title-group.article-title: Intraventricular Cerliponase Alfa Treatment in a Patient with Advanced Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis Type 2

abstract.p: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2 (CLN2) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal disease caused by decreased activity of the enzyme tripeptidyl peptidase 1 (TPP1) due to pathogenic variants in the TPP1 gene. Cerliponase alfa, a recombinant proenzyme form of TPP1, has shown efficacy in preventing motor and language function decline in early-stage CLN2. However, the safety and effects of this therapy in advanced-stage CLN2 are unclear. We herein report a case of intraventricular cerliponase alfa treatment for over a year in a patient with advanced-stage CLN2. The results suggest the safety and potential efficacy of treatment at an advanced stage of CLN2.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN) is an autosomal recessive form of lysosomal disease and is now classified into types 1 to 14 according to genetic abnormalities. CLN type 2 (CLN2) is caused by decreased activity of the lysosomal enzyme tripeptidyl peptidase 1 (TPP1) due to pathogenic variants in the TPP1 gene, leading to the accumulation of intracellular lysosomal metabolites and cell death (1-4). Recently, the efficacy of an enzyme-replacement therapy using cerliponase alfa, a recombinant proenzyme form of human TPP1, has been shown to prevent the progressive decline of the motor and language function in cases of early-stage CLN2 (5) and has been approved in the USA, EU, and other countries, including Japan. However, its safety and clinical efficacy in patients with advanced CLN2 remain unclear.
We herein report a patient with CLN2 at an advanced stage in whom intraventricular cerliponase alfa treatment was administered every two weeks for over a year.

sec.title: Case Report
sec.p: The patient was a 21-year-old man with a history of CLN2 (Fig. 1). The patient had achieved head holding at 3 months old, rolling over at 5 months old, sitting independently at 8 months old, pulling himself up at 9 months old, and walking independently at 14 months old. However, the patient had a language delay, with babbling observed at two years old. At 2 years and 10 months old, afebrile generalized convulsions in flexion of both upper limbs and extension of both lower limbs were observed. Thereafter, seizures occurred every one to two weeks, and the patient visited the hospital.

caption.p: The course of this patient. He was functionally normal until 2 years and 10 months old, although he had a language delay. Subsequently, he developed generalized seizures. Thereafter, his motor, language, and cognitive functions rapidly declined. At three years old, he had spastic paraplegia, cerebellar ataxia, and a decline in his visual function due to retinitis pigmentosa. Detailed investigations were performed, but his diagnosis was still unclear. His seizures became intractable, and he was unable to walk by himself, thus requiring a walking frame at four years old. He was diagnosed with CLN2 at four years and eight months old (see main text). He then developed myoclonus, dysphagia, and recurrent episodes of aspiration pneumonia, necessitating a modified diet and the use of a nasogastric tube for medication. All of these symptoms progressively deteriorated until eight years old, when laryngotrachotomy was performed. Sudden cardiac arrest occurred at eight years and four months old, followed by hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (see main text). Due to severe myoclonus and spasticity, intrathecal baclofen therapy was started at 14 years old and was associated with some improvement in these symptoms. Around the same time, the patient’s mother noticed that the patient exhibited a startle reflex.

sec.p: Although interictal electroencephalography (EEG) and head computed tomography (CT) did not show any abnormalities, because the seizures were repeated, the patient was started on valproic acid. However, the seizures were not controlled, and there was a rapid decline in his motor, language, cognitive, and visual functions. At three years old, he had an obvious wobble when walking and crawling on all fours. Repeat CT of the head showed brain atrophy; therefore, detailed investigations were performed. The patient was diagnosed with slow progressive cognitive decline, progressive cerebellar ataxia (intention tremor and ataxic gait), and acquired visual impairment. Blood (including lactate and amino acid analyses), urine (including organic acid analysis), cerebrospinal fluid, and bone marrow tests, as well as nerve conduction studies, showed no abnormalities. However, head magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed diffuse cerebellar and cerebral cortical atrophy, and EEG showed irregular slow waves and sharp waves from the frontal to central regions during sleep, with spike waves observed in the right frontal region. An ophthalmologic examination revealed optic nerve atrophy and retinal pigment degeneration, the electroretinogram showed flattening, and the visual evoked potential (VEP) showed reduced responses, indicating that both eyes had visual acuity considered to be in the light perception range. At 4 years old, the TPP1 enzyme activity was found to be low (5.4 nmol/mg protein/h, normal range: 390.07±118.5 nmol/mg protein/h), and he was diagnosed with CLN2. His Hamburg Motor and Language (HML) scale (6) was already 1 point each, for a total of 2 points at the time.

Owing to repeated aspiration pneumonia, laryngotracheal separation was performed at eight years old. At nine years old, his mother found that his neck was bent forward, and his airway was obstructed. Ventilation and chest compressions were initiated. After five cycles of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, the patient resumed his heartbeat for 13 minutes. Before this event, the lower limbs showed an equinovarus position, and the upper limbs showed extension with spasticity. After cardiac arrest, the muscle tonus became hypertonic, with the limbs in a flexed position, and the myoclonus appeared semi-persistently, leading to a bedridden state. Botulinum toxin injections were attempted in the lower legs as a treatment for increased muscle tone, but no improvement was observed. There were no significant changes in the EEG findings after cardiopulmonary arrest. At 14 years old, a baclofen intramedullary pump was implanted, and the myoclonus decreased with improvement in muscle tone. The patient's clinical course over the next few years included the development of scoliosis. He had recurrent aspiration pneumonia during his teenage years, likely due to microaspiration. At 17 years old, he developed an influenza virus infection associated with septic shock. Although the patient recovered from this severe infection, he subsequently required home oxygen therapy and nocturnal mechanical ventilation. Up to 21 years old, he experienced generalized epilepsy associated with frequent episodes of status epilepticus. He also had a recurrent fever due to microaspiration or urinary tract infection.

Following the approval of cerliponase alfa treatment in Japan in 2019, the patient was referred from the pediatric department to our adult neurology department for cerliponase alfa treatment. On admission, he was bedridden and non-communicative. Neurological findings included impaired consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale score E1VTM1); loss of brainstem reflexes, such as corneal, pupillary light, ciliospinal, pharyngeal, and cough reflexes; spinal automatism; and hypertonus of all extremities. Contracture was observed in the upper and lower limbs, including the shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, and ankles. Frontal lobe signs (such as snout, palmomental, and sucking reflexes) and the startle reflex were evident. There was no myoclonus, and his HML scale was 0. His medication list included gabapentin 1,800 mg/day, levetiracetam 3,000 mg/day, nitrazepam 4 mg/day, clobazam 12 mg/day, perampanel 4 mg/day, dantrolene 50 mg/day, and diazepam 6 mg/day. However, despite this, he experienced generalized seizures once or twice a week. The patient was also treated with intrathecal baclofen therapy (310 μg/day).

Blood and cerebrospinal fluid examinations revealed no abnormalities. Head MRI showed marked cerebral, brainstem, and cerebellar atrophy (Fig. 2). EEG recordings did not demonstrate any epileptiform discharges; however, interpretation was difficult because of artifacts from respiratory muscle activity. No cortical N20 potentials were detected in somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs). No responses were evoked by visual evoked potentials or auditory brainstem response tests. We also performed genetic testing, which revealed that he was a compound heterozygous variant for the TPP1 known heterozygous variant NM_000391.4(TPP1):c.1016G＞A (p.Arg339Gln) from his father and a TPP1 novel heterozygous variant NM_000391.4(TPP1):c.717C＞A (p.Asp239Glu) from his mother.

caption.p: Brain magnetic resonance imaging findings at 21 years old. There was severe brain atrophy accompanied by low-intensity signals in the deep white matter on T1- and T2-weighted images and high-intensity signals in the thalamus and deep white matter on T2-weighted images.

sec.p: Ethical considerations in this study pertained to the patient's inability to provide his informed consent, resulting in the mother possessing legal authority as the designated surrogate decision-maker, assuming the responsibility of making decisions on behalf of the patient. Considering the cerliponase alfa treatment in this patient, we informed the patient of all possible surgical risks related to device implantation in a patient with severe brain atrophy. Because his mother still wished for him to receive this treatment, we decided to administer cerliponase alfa to this patient.

To monitor the safety and effects of cerliponase alfa, we selected several measures; to detect safety issues, his vital signs, infusion reactions, and signs of device-related infection were carefully monitored. We also checked the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) before and after the cerliponase alfa infusion. To assess the efficacy of the treatment, we evaluated the ventilator withdrawal time, defined as the time required to maintain the patient's percutaneous oxygen saturation above 90% in room air without the use of a ventilator, along with the number of seizures (and status epilepticus). He was started on cerliponase alfa infusion at 20 years and 9 months old. These values were recorded 55 days before the date of the first infusion (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Several clinical measures were monitored to determine the safety and efficacy of cerliponase alfa over four weeks with this patient. The X-axis shows the time before (baseline 1 and 2) and after infusion (every 4 weeks). The Y-axis denotes the fever frequency (/4 weeks) (A), seizure frequency (/4 weeks) (B), and ventilator withdrawal time (h/day, average for 4 weeks) (C). The dashed line indicates the average of the baseline and during treatment.

sec.p: Figure 3 shows the details of these clinical measures before and during the cerliponase alfa treatment. Regarding safety, CSF tests were negative before and after infusion. No apparent device infection was noted during treatment. Premedication consisted of prednisolone (10 mg) and histamine H1-receptor antagonists (5 mg). We observed occasional fever reactions related to cerliponase alfa infusion; however, overall, the frequency of a fever developing decreased with time (Fig. 3A). Regarding seizure frequency, although there was some fluctuation, the average number of seizures (and episodes of status epilepticus) decreased from 5.5/4 weeks at baseline (2 months observation) to 3.4/4 weeks (during treatment) (Fig. 3B). Although we did not make any changes to his medications during this period, the patient did not have status epilepticus after starting cerliponase alfa once a month before treatment. However, it was observed that the ventilator withdrawal time did not change even after one year of treatment.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We encountered a patient with CLN2 at an advanced stage in whom intraventricular cerliponase alfa treatment was administered every two weeks for longer than a year. Before discussing the potential effects of cerliponase alfa, it is important to evaluate the patient's clinical condition. First, he had an atypical, prolonged clinical course with a late infantile onset compared with the typical case of CLN2. Second, due to the severe neurological impact of cardiac arrest and the complete loss of any neurological function (loss of brainstem reflexes), the only neurological symptom that could be evaluated was seizures. However, whether or not these are caused by CLN2 or its origin following brain injury cannot be differentiated. This makes the evaluation of the effect difficult. Usually, seizures at this stage of the disease decrease naturally in frequency and do not require extensive medication, as in our case. Considering the high frequency of seizures, it may be possible that our patient also had non-epileptic myoclonus as well as an epileptic seizure.

A previous study demonstrated that intraventricular cerliponase alfa prevented worsening of the HML scale in 24 patients with CLN2 (5). Three patients were at a relatively late stage of disease. Another study in France showed the effects of cerliponase alfa in seven patients with CLN2, including a patient with an HML score ＜3 points. The authors reported that almost all patients treated with cerliponase alfa had better epilepsy control, allowing for a reduction in antiepileptic medication (7). Consistent with this view, we observed a reduction in seizure frequency in our patient compared with baseline (Fig. 3A). In addition, the same French research showed that 1 out of 8 patients had begun epilepsy after the very beginning of treatment. It has been shown that 96% of patients had convulsions, and 17% had epilepsy as a side effect of cerliponase alfa (5). Whether or not a reduction in seizure frequency from 5.5 to 3.4/4 weeks is clinically relevant for a patient with such a severe neurological condition is unclear. Furthermore, the frequency of seizures is likely to be reduced after cerliponase alfa treatment, and we must acknowledge the presence of concomitant hypoxic encephalopathy; therefore, it is difficult to conclude that cerliponase alfa is effective even in patients with advanced disease. Nevertheless, the present patient had never experienced status epilepticus after starting cerliponase alfa once a month before treatment. We suggest that reduction of seizures, especially status epilepticus may reflect a treatment effect in this patient.

Unexpectedly, the occurrence of a fever was reduced. The reason for this is unclear, although the reduction of seizure frequency and good nursing care during hospital admissions for treatment may have reduced the risk of infections (8,9). It is also possible that this may be related to the use of antipyretic drugs as a premedication. There was no change in the ventilator withdrawal time.

The most common adverse events of intraventricular cerliponase alfa reported are convulsions (96%), pyrexia (71%), vomiting (63%), hypersensitivity reactions (63%), upper respiratory tract infections (54%), nasopharyngitis, and rhinitis (42%) (5). Twelve patients (50%) had 34 device-related adverse events, 3 of which were device-related infections. In our patient, we did not observe any adverse events for 450 days. Therefore, this case is an example of the safe administration of cerliponase alfa in a very severe case of CLN2.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We herein report an advanced case of CLN2 with cerliponase alfa treatment for longer than one year. The treatment was safe, and there seems to have been a reduction in the frequency of seizures and a fever with cerliponase alfa. The reason for this may be multifactorial, but it is possible to assume that cerliponase alfa may be effective in reducing seizure frequency, even in patients with very severe CLN2.
